description: Hi everyone! I’m passionate about space, technology, and software. I aim to develop a health monitoring system for astronauts using data analysis, risk detection, and visualization. I value teamwork, creativity, and learning. I’m looking for curious teammates skilled in coding, hardware, data analysis, web development, design, communication, and space habitats. Let’s combine our skills to make space missions safer!
summary:
Astra is a crew health monitoring web app for astronauts on long-duration missions, built for crew members who are not doctors. A wearable feed (simulated in our prototype) sends readings every 3 minutes: heart rate, blood oxygen, respiration, body temperature, HRV stress indicator, sleep, exercise and radiation exposure. Astra stores the readings in a database and compares them with warning and critical thresholds. It explains each result in plain, guiding language, using an interactive x-ray body map, a live ECG monitor and hourly charts that can be exported to Excel or CSV.

This addresses the challenge by turning raw sensor data into clear steps an astronaut can take on their own. Long missions also strain mental health, so Astra includes a support page focused on missing family and Earth, a text, audio and video journal, mood check-ins, gamified daily tasks and cycle tracking for female crew. Polaris, a Gemini-based assistant, answers questions using the astronaut’s live values as context.

This matters because as missions travel farther from Earth, communication delays grow, and crews must recognize and respond to health problems themselves. Astra runs in any browser and in 14 languages.
details:
What it does and how it works

Astra is a health monitoring system for astronauts on long-duration missions, designed for crew members without medical training. A smartwatch feed (simulated in this prototype) sends readings every 3 minutes: heart rate, blood oxygen, respiratory rate, body temperature, HRV (stress indicator), sleep duration, exercise minutes and radiation exposure. Each reading is stored in a database and compared with warning and critical thresholds. The app then explains the result in plain language and tells the astronaut what to do next.

The app has these main sections:

  • Live Values: an interactive x-ray body map that colors each body region by status, with a thermal view, an animated live ECG monitor, an Earth clock, and environment information (ISS, Moon, Mars).
  • Tasks: gamified daily habits with points, including a water counter, a 90-minute workout timer that can be paused and resumed, and mood check-ins.
  • Charts: daily trends, hourly averages with warning and critical lines, and a 30-minute data table that can be exported to Excel or CSV.
  • Safety & Support: focused on mental health during isolation, especially missing family and Earth, with a “connect home” option and cycle tracking for female crew members.
  • Journal: private entries in text, audio or video, with search and sorting.
  • Polaris: an AI assistant powered by Google Gemini. It receives all of the astronaut’s current values and profile as context, so its answers reflect their real situation. It accepts file, audio and image attachments, and has a chat mode and a task mode.
  • Notifications: alerts in the top bar that lead directly to the relevant page.

Benefits and intended impact

On deep-space missions, communication delays with Earth can reach many minutes, so crews will need to detect and handle health problems themselves. Astra turns raw sensor numbers into clear guidance, supports both physical and mental health in one place, and keeps a structured health record that flight surgeons can export and review. The same approach could also help people in other isolated settings, such as polar stations, submarines or remote workers.

Tools and technologies

  • Language: Python
  • Interface and web app: Streamlit, plus custom HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the ECG canvas, SVG body overlays and live clock
  • Data: SQLite, pandas, NumPy
  • Charts and export: Plotly, openpyxl
  • AI and translation: Google Gemini API (google-genai) for Polaris; deep-translator for automatic translation into 14 languages
  • Images: Pillow, for processing profile photos
  • Deployment: GitHub and Streamlit Community Cloud; PyInstaller for an offline Windows desktop version
  • Design: Figma

No physical hardware was used. The watch data is simulated with realistic day and night, exercise and stress patterns.

What makes it creative

  • It combines a medical-monitor look with an x-ray body map, so status is visible at a glance instead of being buried in tables.
  • It treats loneliness and homesickness as health factors alongside vital signs.
  • The AI assistant does not use fixed scripts. It receives the astronaut’s live data as context, so every answer is personal.
  • Gamified tasks make healthy routines engaging.

Factors the team considered

  • Usability for non-doctors: clear, guiding text, simple navigation, and nothing confusing or overly technical.
  • Mental health: support content focused on family and Earth.
  • Privacy: each user gets a separate database, and the API key is kept in server secrets, not in the code.
  • Inclusivity: 14 languages and female-specific health tracking.
  • Reliability: an offline desktop version that works without internet(except the AI assistant and automatic translation).
  • Clarity: consistent warning and critical color coding throughout the app.

Use of AI tools: Parts of the code were written and debugged with the help of an AI assistant (Claude by Anthropic). Our team designed, reviewed, tested and deployed the app. Inside the app, the Polaris assistant uses the Google Gemini API.
